client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... can't bring myself to go, because being around everyone just makes her absence feel even more overwhelming. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist:
It takes real courage to reach out even when you're not sure it will help, and I'm really glad you did. The pain you're describing — where the people who love you most can actually make the loss feel sharper — makes complete sense, because family gatherings hold so many memories of her. 

I'm curious, when you imagine walking into one of those get-togethers, what's the very first thought that comes to mind?

client: When I picture walking in, the first thing I think is that she should be there. It's like my brain does this quick scan of the room and just... notices the absence before anything else, before I even say hello to anyone. And then I feel this wave of guilt, like I should be happy to see everyone, but instead I'm already fighting back tears before I've even taken my coat off.
therapist:
That moment you're describing — your mind instinctively searching for her before you've even settled in — is such a profound testament to how much she meant to you, and it's not a flaw in your thinking, it's love. The guilt you feel for not being "happy enough" is really worth gently examining, because grieving her presence and being glad to see your family aren't actually opposites — they can exist in the same moment. 

What do you think your grandmother would say if she knew you were carrying that guilt?

client: I've thought about that before, and honestly, I think she'd tell me to stop being ridiculous and just enjoy being with the people I love. But then I immediately feel like I'm just... making up what she'd say to let myself off the hook, you know? Like I don't actually deserve to feel better that easily.
therapist:
That second-guessing voice is really worth noticing — you had a genuinely warm and probably quite accurate sense of who she was and how she'd respond, and then something immediately moved to take that comfort away from you. It sounds like there might be a belief underneath all of this that you need to *earn* the right to feel better, as though grieving harder somehow honors her more. 

Where do you think that idea — that feeling better means you're letting yourself off the hook — might have come from?

client: I don't know, maybe it goes back to how our family handled loss. Nobody ever really talked about moving on or feeling okay — it was like the sadness was proof that you loved someone, and if you stopped being sad, it meant you didn't care enough. I guess I absorbed that without even realizing it, and now it feels almost disloyal to have a good day or laugh at something without immediately feeling guilty about it.
therapist:
What a profound insight — you've just uncovered a kind of unwritten family rule that equates love with suffering, and recognizing that it was *absorbed* rather than consciously chosen is really important, because it means it isn't simply the truth. The loyalty you feel toward her is so clearly real and deep, and it's worth gently asking whether she would actually want her legacy to be that you can never laugh or have a good day again. 

If you could imagine a different way of honoring her — one that didn't require you to suffer — what might that look like to you?

client: I've never really thought about it that way before, and honestly it kind of catches me off guard. Like, part of me wants to push back and say that suffering is just what love looks like when someone's gone, that's just how grief works. But then I think about my mom and who she actually was, and she was someone who laughed a lot, who wanted people around her to be okay, and maybe you're right that she wouldn't have wanted this for me.
therapist:
That moment of holding both things at once — the old belief pulling you back, and this newer, truer sense of who she actually was — that's not confusion, that's real growth happening in real time. It sounds like somewhere beneath the grief, you already carry a version of her that laughs, that wants you to be okay, and that part of her doesn't have to be lost just because she is. 

I'm wondering — what might it feel like to bring *that* version of her with you to the next family gathering, almost like she's rooting for you from the inside rather than being the absence you're scanning the room for?

client: That's... a really beautiful way to put it, and part of me wants to hold onto that image. But honestly, when I'm actually at one of those gatherings and everyone's talking around the space where she used to be, I don't know if I can just summon that feeling on demand — it sounds easier in this room than it will be in that kitchen. I'm a little worried that if I try and it doesn't work, I'll just feel more alone, like I failed at grieving the right way too.
therapist:
You're absolutely right to name that gap between insight and the messy reality of being in that kitchen — it would be unfair of me to suggest that a beautiful idea automatically becomes easy to feel in a hard moment, and your skepticism is actually really healthy. But I want to gently push back on one thing: if you go and it's painful and the feeling doesn't come, that isn't failing at grief, that's just grief — it's allowed to be hard even when you're trying. 

What if instead of going with the goal of *feeling* differently, you went with the much smaller goal of just staying for a little while and seeing what happens — taking the pressure of "doing it right" completely off the table?

client: I hear what you're saying, and taking the pressure off does sound more manageable in theory. But I think part of me is scared that even "just staying" will feel like too much, like I'll walk in and just want to leave immediately and then feel guilty for not being able to handle it. It's like no matter how small I make the goal, I find a way to feel like I'm doing it wrong.
therapist:
What you just described — this pattern where the goalposts keep moving so that you're always just out of reach of "doing it right" — that's such an important thing to notice, because it suggests the problem isn't the size of the goal, it's that there's a part of you that isn't quite ready to let yourself off the hook yet, no matter what. Even leaving early after five minutes would actually be *brave*, not a failure — you showed up, you felt something real, and you took care of yourself. 

I'm curious, whose voice does it sound like when it tells you that you're doing it wrong — is it yours, or does it remind you of anyone?

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because honestly... it sounds like my dad. He had this way of pointing out everything you did slightly wrong, not in a cruel way exactly, but like there was always a better version of you that you were failing to be. And I guess I never really connected that to how I talk to myself now, but sitting here I can feel how similar it sounds.
therapist:
That pause you just took is really significant — you've just made a connection that many people spend years not seeing, between a voice that was outside you then and one that feels like *you* now, but maybe never fully was. It makes so much sense that grief would amplify that voice, because loss can strip away our defenses and leave us more vulnerable to our oldest, most deeply learned ways of seeing ourselves. 

How does it feel to recognize that the harshest critic in the room might be someone else's voice you've been carrying around as your own?

client: It feels... strange, honestly, like a weird kind of relief mixed with something that almost makes me want to cry. Because if it's not really my voice, then maybe I'm not as broken as I thought — but then I also don't know who I am without it, because it's been there for so long. I'm not sure I even know what my own voice sounds like anymore.
therapist:
That mix of relief and grief you're feeling right now makes complete sense, because you're not just mourning your grandmother in this moment — you're also beginning to mourn a version of yourself that was defined by that critical voice, and that's its own kind of loss. But the fact that you can already distinguish between that voice and something that feels truer and kinder — the part that remembered your grandmother's laugh, that knew she'd want you to be okay — that *is* your voice, and it's been here this whole time. 

I wonder, if you tried to describe what that quieter, kinder voice inside you sounds like when it does manage to speak up, what would you say?

client: I think... that quieter voice sounds a lot like exhaustion, honestly — like it's tired of fighting and just wants to rest for a second. It doesn't say grand things, it just sometimes whispers something like "you're doing the best you can" when I'm really worn down. But I'm not sure I actually believe it when it says that — it feels more like something I'm supposed to think than something I really feel.
therapist:
That whisper — "you're doing the best you can" — might feel borrowed or hollow right now, but I want you to notice that it's still there, still showing up even when you're exhausted, and that's not nothing. Sometimes our kinder voice speaks quietly and unconvincingly at first, not because it's wrong, but because it's newer and less practiced than the critical one that's had decades of repetition. 

I'm curious — can you think of one specific moment recently, even a small one, where looking back you can see that you actually *were* doing the best you could, even if it didn't feel that way at the time?
